entries.definition: a proposed explanation that can be tested
entries.example: The hypothesis predicts a difference between the two conditions.

entries.definition: based on observation or experiment rather than belief alone
entries.example: The claim needs empirical support before we rely on it.

entries.definition: relating to an explanatory model rather than direct practical testing
entries.example: The theoretical model helps us decide what to measure.

entries.definition: to obtain a result again by following the original method
entries.example: Another team tried to reproduce the result using the published instructions.

entries.definition: to repeat a study or test to examine its findings
entries.translation: تکرار کردن یک پژوهش یا آزمایش
entries.example: The class will replicate the experiment with new samples.

entries.definition: to express something as a measured amount
entries.example: The survey attempts to quantify how often delays occur.

entries.definition: to adjust a measuring instrument against a known standard
entries.example: We calibrate the scale before comparing the samples.

entries.definition: the closeness of repeated measurements to one another
entries.example: Similar repeated readings showed good precision, even before we checked accuracy.

entries.definition: the extent to which a value or outcome is not known exactly
entries.example: The report states the uncertainty instead of presenting a perfectly exact value.

entries.definition: a pattern in which two measured things vary together
entries.example: The correlation does not by itself explain why the changes happened.

entries.definition: a relationship in which one thing produces a change in another
entries.example: Showing causation requires more than noticing that two events occur together.

entries.definition: a measure of how likely an event is
entries.example: The probability estimate depends on the assumptions in the model.

entries.definition: selected or occurring without a predictable chosen pattern
entries.example: Each participant received a random number before the groups were formed.

entries.definition: a systematic influence that can distort a judgment or result
entries.example: Choosing only enthusiastic volunteers could introduce bias into the survey.

entries.definition: the share of a whole represented by one part
entries.example: The proportion of shaded ground increased as the tree grew.

entries.definition: how often an event or repeating change occurs
entries.example: We counted the frequency of interruptions during each session.

entries.definition: the way values or items are spread across a group or area
entries.example: The average hides important differences in the distribution of journey times.

entries.definition: reflecting the important characteristics of a larger group
entries.example: A representative sample should not include only the easiest people to reach.

entries.definition: to separate one factor so it can be examined
entries.example: The experiment tries to isolate the effect of light.

entries.definition: the process through which something produces an effect
entries.example: The observations suggest a mechanism but do not fully establish it.

entries.definition: an event or process that can be observed
entries.example: The unusual phenomenon led the students to ask new questions.

entries.definition: a characteristic of a material or substance
entries.example: Density is a useful property when comparing materials.

entries.definition: the substances or parts that something contains
entries.example: The rock’s composition helps explain its appearance.

entries.definition: a substance formed from chemically combined elements
entries.example: Water is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen.

entries.definition: a group of bonded atoms acting as a unit
entries.example: The model represents a molecule with connected colored balls.

entries.definition: a basic unit of a chemical element
entries.example: Each color in the diagram represents a different kind of atom.

entries.definition: a very small piece of matter
entries.example: A fine particle of dust was visible in the beam of light.

entries.definition: a negatively charged particle associated with atoms
entries.example: The diagram uses an arrow to represent electron movement.

entries.definition: the central part of an atom
entries.example: The model places the nucleus at the center of the atom.

entries.definition: energy traveling as waves or particles
entries.example: The sensor measures a particular kind of radiation.

entries.definition: the distance between matching points in a repeating wave
entries.example: The illustration compares light with a longer and shorter wavelength.

entries.definition: the range of wavelengths or frequencies in a signal or radiation
entries.example: The prism helps reveal part of the visible spectrum.

entries.definition: to take in energy or a substance
entries.example: Dark surfaces can absorb more light than similar light-colored ones.

entries.definition: to change the direction of light as it enters another material
entries.example: A glass prism can refract light into different directions.

entries.definition: to release energy or a substance
entries.example: The instrument detects light that hot objects emit.

entries.definition: to allow heat or electricity to pass through
entries.example: Copper can conduct electricity, so it is used in many wires.

entries.definition: to reduce the movement of heat, sound, or electricity
entries.example: A suitable layer can insulate the container against heat loss.

entries.definition: the amount of mass in a particular volume
entries.example: Two blocks of the same size can have different density.

entries.definition: the amount of space occupied by something
entries.example: The container’s volume determines how much water it can hold.

entries.definition: the amount of matter in an object
entries.example: The balance compares the mass of the two samples.

entries.definition: resistance when surfaces move against one another
entries.example: Friction between the tires and road helps a bicycle stop.

entries.definition: a state in which opposing effects are balanced
entries.example: The hanging model remained in equilibrium until we moved a weight.

entries.definition: a change in velocity over time
entries.example: The graph shows acceleration as the cart begins to move.

entries.definition: speed measured together with a direction
entries.example: A change in direction changes velocity even at the same speed.

entries.definition: the curved path of one body around another in space
entries.example: The diagram shows a satellite’s orbit around Earth.

entries.definition: the layer of gases surrounding a planet
entries.example: Earth’s atmosphere affects how the sky looks from the ground.

entries.definition: change in inherited characteristics of populations over generations
entries.example: The lesson explains evolution using differences across many generations.

entries.definition: an inherited feature that helps an organism in its environment
entries.example: The thick covering is an adaptation that can reduce water loss.

entries.definition: an individual living thing
entries.example: A microscope helped us observe the tiny organism.

entries.definition: related to inherited biological information
entries.example: The article distinguishes genetic differences from changes caused by conditions.
